Abstract
Heavy alkali-metal treatments have been the most recent breakthrough in improving
the efficiency of Cu(In,Ga)Se2 (CIGS) solar cells. Alkali halides are generally evapo-
rated onto the surface of the CIGS thin film by a vacuum process. Here, we report an
alternative, low-cost solution process for the surface treatment of CIGS thin films
using cesium carbonate (CsCO3) as a new route to incorporate cesium (Cs) for
improving solar cell performance. CIGS thin films were fabricated using pulsed hybrid
reactive magnetron sputtering and the surface treatment was performed by spin-
coating CsCO3 solution on the surface of CIGS at room temperature, followed by
vacuum annealing at 400C. The surface chemistry of the CIGS thin film changed
after the treatment and the efficiency of respective solar cells improved by more than
30%, mostly driven by an enhancement in open-circuit voltage. X-ray photoelectron
spectroscopy revealed the depletion of copper and the presence of Cs on the surface
of the CIGS thin film. Ultraviolet photoelectron spectroscopy showed the lowering of
the valence band maximum by around 0.25 eV after the treatment, which plays a
positive role in reducing interfacial recombination. High-resolution transmission elec-
tron microscopy indicates the presence of Cs and depletion of Cu at the grain bound-
aries of the CIGS thin film. These findings open a low-cost route for improving the
performance of CIGS solar cells by surface modification using a solution process.

multi-junction solar cells.4–6 Typically, the heavy alkali metal (such as

ing an alkali-fluoride (AlkF) after the deposition of the CIGS thin film,
known as a post-deposition treatment (PDT).11–26

efficiency of CIGS thin film solar cells are summarized in Figure 1.

Owing to the effective Cd diffusion, a thinner CdS layer is facilitated,
decreasing parasitic absorption and increasing the short-circuit current

imum at the CIGS surface, repelling holes from reaching the buffer/

increases the net hole concentration in the CIGS bulk due to substitu-
tion of donor-type (point) defects (InCu) and/or line defect (dislocations)
with alkali metals.20,21 An increased open-circuit voltage (VOC) of the
device is achieved due to the change in the net hole concentration
before (N0) and after (NA) the treatment.20–23 (iv) Heavy alkali metals
passivate the CIGS grain boundaries by the formation of alkali com-
pounds.18,21 As a result, both the minority carrier lifetime and photolu-
minescence intensity increase,20,22,24 validating the material's suitability
for high-performance solar cells.20–25
To date, alkali-halides (e.g, KF, RbF, etc.) are used almost exclu-
sively as alkali sources, generally deposited on the surface of the CIGS
thin film immediately after deposition by vacuum evaporation, known
as the alkali-fluoride (AlkF) post-deposition treatment (PDT).11–26
There are few reports about solution processes to provide alkali
elements, which also improve device performance. The authors
spin-coated KF27 or KI28 after absorber growth followed by annealing
in N2 or Se atmosphere. However, a detailed investigation of the
solution-processed samples at grains and grain boundaries and about
the diffusion of the alkali elements into the absorber layer has yet to
be performed.
The present work demonstrates a low-cost solution process for
incorporating Cs into CIGS thin films using cesium carbonate (CsCO3).
This CsCO3 solution treatment (Cs-ST) modifies the CIGS surface and
changes the surface property from hydrophilic to hydrophobic nature. A
controlled amount of spin-coated CsCO3 improves the solar cell's open-
circuit voltage (VOC), fill factor (FF), and efficiency (ɳ) similar to the well-
established evaporation processes of alkali-halides. X-ray photoelectron
spectroscopy (XPS) measurements confirm the formation of a Cu-
depleted surface layer of the CIGS thin film after the Cs-ST process.
Ultraviolet photoelectron spectroscopy (UPS) measurements reveal a
lowering of the valence band, and high-resolution transmission electron
microscopy (HRTEM) measurements confirm the presence of Cs at the
grain boundaries close to the surface of the CIGS thin film but much less
deeper inside the absorber layer. The improvements in the photovoltaic
parameters upon the Cs-ST are similar to those observed with the stan-
dard CsF-PDT process in vacuum.29–31 On the other hand, CsCO3 has
been widely used in the past in the fabrication of various electronic
devices.32–37 It mainly induces n-type doping, alters the energy level of
semiconductors and lowers the work function of metal electrodes.32–39
These effects are typically attributed to the formation of an X-O-Cs
(X = In, Ga, Si, W, C) surface termination.40–42

RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
SEM images of Cs-ST and untreated CIGS thin films after rinsing with
DI water (Figure 2) show no significant changes in the surface
morphology upon the Cs-ST, indicating that CsCO3 did not form a
visible inseparable layer as observed for the CsF-PDT of CIGS in
vacuum.28–30 Nevertheless, XPS spectra of the CIGS thin films with
(red curve) and without (black curve) Cs-ST (Figure 2C) clearly show
two additional peaks at binding energies of 723 and 737 eV for the
Cs-ST sample, corresponding to the Cs 3d5/2 and Cs 3d3/2 lines,
respectively, which confirms the presence of Cs at the surface of the
Cs-ST CIGS thin films.
To get further insights into the change of the surface properties,
detailed XPS spectra of the Cu 2p3/2, In 3d5/2, Ga 2p3/2, Se 3d, and Cs
3d5/2 peaks were measured (Figure 3). These spectra reveal that Cu is
depleted at the near-surface region in the Cs-ST CIGS thin film (solid
lines) as compared to the untreated CIGS film (dotted lines). After
sputter-etching the CIGS thin film to a depth of around 40 nm, the Cu
peak intensity of the Cs-ST sample coincides with that of the
untreated CIGS thin film, suggesting the formation of a Cu-deficient
layer of around 40 nm at the surface of the Cs-ST sample. Similarly,
the peak intensity of In 3d5/2 (Figure 3B), Ga 2p3/2 (Figure 3C), and Se
3d (Figure 3D) decreased at the very near surface region (0 nm) and
increased when going deeper (> 20 nm). In our sample, even after DI
water rinsing, the intensity of the Ga 2p3/2 peak did not reduce, indi-
cating that the change of surface properties in Cs-ST CIGS is different
from that of AlkF-PDT CIGS.11 The peak intensity of Cs 3d5/2
(Figure 3E), on the other hand, increased at the surface region, indicat-
ing the formation of a Cs-related layer at the surface.

CONCLUSION
In summary, we presented an alternative to the vacuum-based
AlkF-PDT by a solution-based PDT using a CsCO3 solution (Cs-ST).
No major changes in the surface morphology of the Cs-ST CIGS thin
films were observed. Nevertheless, XPS measurements confirm the
presence of Cs at the surface region and a lowering of the VBM by
around 0.25 eV for the Cs-ST sample. HR-TEM indicates the presence
of Cs and depletion of Cu at the grain boundaries of the CIGS thin film
only up to a depth of a few hundred nanometers from the surface.
Unlike the vacuum Alk-PDT, our Cs-ST process prevents Cs from
reaching the CIGS/Mo interface, which prevents the related lowering
of the VBM at the CIGS/Mo interface.
